introduction: “There are only four accepted criteria of comprehension”: the senses, reason, tradition, and inspiration. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá gave this analysis many times, to philosophers, to freethinkers and at his own table, and each time took the criteria apart. The senses mistake a mirage for water; reasoners contradict one another; tradition has to be understood by reason and shares its fallibility; inspiration cannot be told from the promptings of self. None is certain. His conclusion is not scepticism. When several criteria agree the proof is strong, and beyond them is a standard that does not err, the bounty of the Holy Spirit. The argument has a long history. The Buddha gave the Kalamas a similar list of things not to rely on; Socrates, Descartes, Pascal and Kant each began from the limits of one way of knowing; Paul says we “know in part”; John says to “try the spirits.” Hume and Locke speak for evidence and for reason as final judges, which is the position the readings examine most closely.
questions: Give an example from your own experience of each criterion failing: the senses, reasoning, a received tradition, a strong inner conviction.
Locke: “Reason must be our last judge.” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses arguments to show that reason errs. Is that a contradiction? What role is left to reason?
“Inspiration” and “the whisperings of Satan” feel alike. What tests do the last reading and John’s “try the spirits” suggest?
When the four criteria agree, the reading calls the result trustworthy. On what question that matters to you do they agree, and on what do they pull apart?

outside.why: “The first criterion is that of the senses.” Aristotle starts his inquiry into knowledge from the senses and from this sentence: all men by nature desire to know.
The senses err; the reading gives the mirage as its example. The Qur’án uses the same one: a mirage in a desert. The thirsty one supposeth it to be water till he cometh unto it and findeth it naught.
Intuition is “a power or a light” by which realities are perceived without the outward senses. Proverbs: the spirit of man is the candle of the Lord, searching all the inward parts.
“Reality is limited to the perception” of the observer. Saxe’s blind men each touched one part of the elephant, and disputed about a creature not one of them has seen.

Scientists and philosophers hold that knowledge comes by observation. Hume, the strictest of them: a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence. The readings accept the rule and question the evidence. What follows from Hume’s rule if no single kind of evidence is certain?

The measures of understanding are sense, reason, tradition and inspiration, and each can fail. The Buddha went through a similar list for the Kalamas: don’t go by reports, by legends, by traditions, by scripture, by logical conjecture, by inference.
Tradition has to be understood by reason, and so inherits reason’s faults. Montaigne: there is more ado to interpret interpretations than to interpret things.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá shows a gathering of rationalists that the philosophers, all reasoning, contradict one another. Locke had staked everything on it: reason must be our last judge and guide in every thing. If reason is fallible, what is left to judge by? Does the argument against reason use reason?
A third way of apprehending truth lies beyond sense and argument. Pascal: the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
Western philosophers hold sense to be the criterion. Descartes began modern philosophy by doubting it: never to accept anything for true which I did not clearly know to be such.
The four standards “are faulty and inaccurate. All of them are liable to mistake.” Paul: now we see through a glass, darkly; now I know in part.
Socrates made the admission the beginning of wisdom: he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows. I neither know nor think that I know.
None of the standards deserves “implicit confidence”; yet the reading does not end in doubt. Kant, after his critique of reason: I must, therefore, abolish knowledge, to make room for belief.
The reading points to the Holy Spirit as the standard that does not err. Jesus: when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth.
When all four criteria agree, the proof is as sure as can be had. The old rule of evidence works by agreement too: in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may be established.
Inspiration and “the whisperings of Satan” both arrive as inclinations of the heart. John: believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.
Paul on why the test is needed: Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light.
